Area.evidence_source: The suicidal state was described as one of misery, hopelessness, gloom, and emotional pain. Despair was characterized by constant negativity and pessimism and became the lens through which the world was interpreted. Interpersonal difficulties, negative life events, and the accompanying pain became overwhelming, leading to a sense of futility and defeat. No goals, plans, or vision of the future seemed possible and participants saw no reason for living. Perceptions of lack of control over life events and emotional experiences were commonly reported. A strong feeling of worthlessness and the belief of not deserving to be loved, cared for, or treated well by others was reported by most participants. Shame of having suicidal feelings and what was characterized as "a mental illness" were commonly reported. Powerful feelings of shame served to reinforce negative self-perceptions. Many participants described perceiving themselves as "bad people" because of the inability to deal effectively with their emotional problems and disclosed powerful feelings of self-loathing and self-hatred. Shame over emotional difficulties was described as contributing to anxiety that commonly arose when participants were around other people. Overall, shame, worthlessness, and anxiety over being exposed impeded many participants' capacity to ask for assistance. Feelings of alienation and personal isolation were consistently reported. Overwhelmingly, participants felt that they were different from those with whom they interacted, that they did not fit in to the social structures around them, and that no one understood them as a person. Emotional and social isolation was experienced through lack of connection to others and through limited experiences of care, love, and intimacy. Feelings of loneliness and abandonment were common, and as they struggled with suicidal feelings, participants also reported increasing withdrawal from those around them.
